name: Umar Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, no problem. Just so you know, I talk fast when I'm nervous.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing electrical engineering, so it's circuits lectures Monday to Thursday and a lab on Friday that eats the whole afternoon. I share a flat with two lads, Tomás and Jun, and the rent is 380 a month each. Three evenings a week I stack shelves at Fenwick's supermarket on Calder Street until ten. I also got elected as a course rep, which mostly means I send a lot of emails about broken equipment in the lab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, less hype to deal with. At Fenwick's, my shift lead Marcus would say the same thing he's said for a year: the self-checkouts and the stock app already cut hours and nothing new is coming. I'd still moan online that companies pretend software is magic so they can cut staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the main thing is that my hours at Fenwick's have already dropped from four evenings to three. If that keeps happening in a plateau world, I'm short on rent by February. My degree feels safe, my part-time job doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marcus for a Saturday shift to make up the hours and start looking at a second job, maybe tutoring maths to school kids. I'd keep using the AI model for debugging my circuit simulations, like I do now, but only to check my work. And I'd stick to the budget spreadsheet Tomás made us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. Nothing is on fire, but I'm one dropped shift away from a bad month, and that's just being a student with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies pretend software is magic. Who do you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners and the investors, not the people on the shelves. They sell a story to the shareholders and the workers pay for it. I'd want stronger rules on how many hours a supermarket has to give people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the hours drop again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and the gym, easy. After that, the train home at Christmas, and I'd tell my dad Idris I can't come. He drives the number 14 bus and he'd tell me not to skip it, which would make me feel worse.

say: I'd say it's good there's less **hype**, but companies still use software as an excuse to cut staff.
At the supermarket I'd back Marcus's view that hours are already **shrinking**.
think: My hours at Fenwick's already fell from four evenings to three, so **rent** is the real problem.
The degree feels safe; the **part-time job** doesn't.
do: Ask Marcus for a **Saturday shift** to replace the lost evening.
Start tutoring school kids in maths for extra cash.
Stick to the shared flat **budget** spreadsheet.
feel: **Tense**; I'm one dropped shift away from a bad month.
S0.quote: I'm one dropped shift away from a bad month, and that's just being a student with no savings.
fieldNote: His worry is the supermarket job, where **automation** has already cut his hours; the degree feels safe.
Blames owners and investors, wants rules on guaranteed **hours** for shift workers.
Uses AI only to check his simulations, an example of careful, steady adoption.

steps.text: Ask Marcus for a Saturday shift at Fenwick's
Tutor school kids in maths on Sunday mornings
Cut takeaways and the gym to protect the rent
Use the AI model to check my circuit simulations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the real fight is, and I'd say it loudly as a course rep. Companies will use it to hire fewer graduates and push the rest harder. I'd want the engineering department to teach us how to work alongside these tools, plus clear rules from the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the junior coding and checking jobs go first, and electrical work for firms like the ones that make controllers includes a lot of both. I'd probably still get a job because I have top grades, but I think half my friends on the course won't, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the department's committee and ask for a module on automation and controls, since robots spread slowly in hands-on work. I'd use the AI tools more, properly, to build projects for a portfolio. And I'd go for a summer placement at a firm that fits hardware and software, because that's the safer middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but also kind of interested. I'm angry for people who won't get the chance, and a bit relieved that I've got decent grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half your friends won't get jobs. What makes you say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the biggest local firm, Calder Controls, took six graduates when it used to take fifteen. That was in the careers talk. If they all use assistants to write the routine code, I can see the number staying at six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to those friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my flatmate Jun to start building real projects now, not wait for lectures, and to join the student union's jobs campaign. I'd also say it's not his fault, because the market's shrinking, not him.

say: I'd say this is the **real fight**, and I'd say it loudly as a course rep.
I'd demand clear **government rules** and teaching on working alongside AI tools.
think: Junior coding and **checking** jobs go first, and my field has lots of both.
I'd probably be fine because of my grades, but half my friends **won't** be.
do: Push the department for a **controls and automation** module.
Use AI tools properly to build **portfolio** projects.
Aim for a summer placement at a firm mixing hardware and software.
feel: **Nervous** but interested, angry on behalf of people who won't get the chance.
S1.quote: Last year the biggest local firm, Calder Controls, took six graduates when it used to take fifteen.
fieldNote: Turns personal worry into **collective** action as a course rep; the group matters more to him than his own odds.
Uses concrete evidence, the local firm's graduate numbers, rather than general fear.
Plans a **hardware plus software** middle path because robots reach hands-on work later.

steps.text: Ask the department to add a controls and automation module
Build three portfolio projects using AI tools to speed me up
Take on extra hardware-focused modules in second year
Apply for a summer placement at Calder Controls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a catastrophe being run by a handful of companies with no democratic say. I'd organise something, a student union meeting at least, to demand a basic income and a freeze on cutting graduate roles. I'd be on every platform telling people to vote on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree is in trouble and the supermarket is too. By 2031 the robots take over the shelves as well. I'd be a graduate in 2029 with a loan and no junior jobs, which isn't a plan, it's a trap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the student union and get a petition running within a week, and I'd keep the degree going because there's no better option. I'd work every extra shift I could get and send my parents nothing. And I'd learn every AI tool I can, to be useful to whoever's still hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd probably be sleeping badly, and I'd tell nobody except Jun. It's a mix of anger and a feeling of being a pawn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, would you still finish the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish it, because dropping out with the loan and nothing to show would be worse. But I'd look at shorter paths too, like a hardware technician qualification, which I could do alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad Idris would say work hard and don't panic, and my mum would be quietly terrified. I'd probably tell them I've got it handled, which wouldn't be true, so I'd be carrying that as well.

say: I'd call it a **catastrophe** run by a few companies with no democratic say.
I'd push for a **basic income** and a freeze on cutting graduate roles.
think: By 2029 I'd graduate into a market with a loan and **no junior jobs**.
The supermarket goes too once **robots** reach shelves around 2031.
do: Start a **petition** through the student union within a week.
Work every extra shift available and save every wage.
Learn as many AI tools as possible to stay useful.
feel: **Alarmed**, sleeping badly, with a feeling of being a pawn.
S2.quote: I'd be a graduate in 2029 with a loan and no junior jobs, which isn't a plan, it's a trap.
fieldNote: Fast turn to **political** action: petition, union meeting, basic income demand.
Hides his fear from his parents, a gap between what he'd say and what he'd feel.
Keeps the degree, while quietly planning a shorter **technician** route as insurance.

steps.text: Write and launch a student petition for a graduate jobs freeze
Call a student union meeting on basic income
Work every extra Fenwick's shift and save the wages
Learn three AI coding and design tools this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and we'd better use it. I'd lobby for retraining funds and for engineering firms to hire more apprentices. At Fenwick's I'd tell my colleagues to start saving, even though nobody wants to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd finish the degree around 2029 and enter a hard market, but I'd have a real shot with a placement and a portfolio. The danger is in 2031, when everything thinking-based is done by machines. Hands-on field engineering lasts a few years longer, around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a placement year if the course allows it, and I'd choose projects where I'm working with real hardware, like motor drives and sensors. I'd keep the supermarket job part-time but save half my pay every month. And I'd keep using the AI tools to build things quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. I can see a route, but a lot rests on the placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said save half your pay. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with rent at 380. Maybe a quarter, honestly, and only if my hours hold. But I'd rather say a number and try than say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to the idea that a degree might not matter by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it still matters, because the person who understands what the machine built is going to be needed. Someone has to sign off a motor controller before it goes into a lift, and I'd like to be that person.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** and we should use it.
I'd lobby for **retraining funds** and more engineering apprenticeships.
think: I'd graduate into a **hard market**, but a placement and portfolio give me a real shot.
Hands-on field engineering should last a few years longer than **desk work**.
do: Do a **placement year** working with motor drives and sensors.
Save a **quarter** of each supermarket pay packet.
Keep using AI tools to build projects quickly.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, because I can see a route.
S3.quote: Someone has to sign off a motor controller before it goes into a lift, and I'd like to be that person.
fieldNote: Five years lets him move from **protest** to practical planning, with a placement as the key step.
Honest about the savings plan being unrealistic at his rent, then offers a smaller number.
Believes **human sign-off** on safety-critical hardware keeps engineers needed.

steps.text: Apply for a placement year working on motor drives
Save a quarter of every Fenwick's pay packet
Build a sensor project using AI tools for the code
Lobby the department for apprenticeship links with local firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's long enough to get it right, if governments don't waste it. I'd probably join a campaign for a national retraining guarantee and mention it at the student union. At Fenwick's I'd say nothing much, because people there only think a month ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have a normal career start, then a very different second half. I might be running automated systems rather than building circuits, and I'd need to keep studying. The worry is that if everyone's told they have ten years, nobody does anything for nine of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the full degree, do a placement, and then probably a master's in control systems. I'd keep a little AI practice going every week, nothing dramatic. And I'd stay involved in the union side, because ten years is how long it takes to change a law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. I'd still be worried about the debt, but it'd feel like normal life with a big question mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody does anything for nine years. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the honest bit. I'd say I would, but I'd probably put things off like everyone else. Having a student union group keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you like to be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Designing safety systems for trains or lifts, with a team around me. I'd want to be someone who makes sure the automatic stuff doesn't hurt anyone.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right, if governments don't **waste** it.
I'd campaign for a national **retraining guarantee**.
think: I'd get a normal career start, then a very different **second half**.
If everyone's told they have ten years, nobody acts for **nine** of them.
do: Finish the full degree and a **placement**, then consider a control systems master's.
Practise with AI tools a little every week.
Stay active in the student union's jobs campaign.
feel: **Settled**, with debt worry and a big question mark.
S4.quote: If everyone's told they have ten years, nobody does anything for nine of them.
fieldNote: Ten years lowers the temperature, but he **distrusts** his own tendency to procrastinate.
Sees the union group as a way to stay honest about acting early.
Imagines a future in **safety systems** where humans remain accountable.

steps.text: Finish the degree and plan a master's in control systems
Spend an hour a week practising with AI tools
Campaign for a national retraining guarantee
Stay on the student union jobs campaign committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't enough for governments or families to do anything, and I'd be graduating into the middle of it. What would help is a proper retraining guarantee, shift workers getting guaranteed hours, and employers being made to keep taking graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that being a course rep has made me see how many people on my course are quietly scared. They don't say it. A place to say it would help, even a group chat with a careers adviser in it.

headlineQuote: Being a course rep has made me see how many people on my course are quietly scared.
portrait: **Umar** is an eighteen-year-old electrical engineering student, a course rep who stacks supermarket shelves three evenings a week.
He's steady with change: uses **AI tools** sometimes, adopts them once they're proven, and blames owners and investors, not technology.
His thin cushion shows in every scenario, from shrinking supermarket **hours** to graduating with a loan.
In the fast scenario he organises **petitions** and demands basic income; with more time he plans placements and control systems.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because he'd graduate into the middle of it with a loan and no junior jobs.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining guarantee**, guaranteed hours for shift workers, and employers obliged to keep hiring graduates.
